```{r setup, include = FALSE}
                      dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
```

The previous vignette introduced flower plots with discrete distributions
(ratings on a 1-7 scale), where each value is a petal. This one is about
**histogram data**, the `MatH` objects of the **HistDAWass** package, where
each cell is the distribution of a continuous variable and the petals become
**violins**. Three examples show what flower plots of histograms are good at,
and the choices that make them readable.

```{r}
library(DistrViz)
library(HistDAWass)
```

## From a histogram to a violin petal

A histogram is first divided into `n_levels` classes of equal width over the
range of the variable (see the first vignette). For flower plots the default
is 30 classes, more than for the other plots, because the profile of the
petal must follow the shape of the distribution. Each class is a slice of the
petal, as wide as its probability and coloured as its position in the range;
the profile of the slices is then smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of standard
deviation `smooth` (in classes, default 1.5). Only the profile is smoothed,
not the colours.

The three flowers below show the same unit of the `BLOOD` data with 10
classes and no smoothing, with the defaults, and with 60 classes and a
stronger smoothing:

```{r, fig.width = 3, fig.height = 3.3, out.width = "32%", fig.show = "hold"}
flower_plot(BLOOD, row = 1, n_levels = 10, smooth = 0, palette = "Zissou 1",
            title = "10 classes, no smoothing") +
  ggplot2::labs(caption = NULL)
flower_plot(BLOOD, row = 1, palette = "Zissou 1", title = "defaults (30, 1.5)") +
  ggplot2::labs(caption = NULL)
flower_plot(BLOOD, row = 1, n_levels = 60, smooth = 3, palette = "Zissou 1",
            title = "60 classes, smooth = 3") +
  ggplot2::labs(caption = NULL)
```

Few classes give a coarse, stepped petal; many classes with a small amount
of smoothing give a profile close to the density of the histogram.

## Population pyramids lying on their side

`Age_Pyramids_2014` contains, for 229 countries, the histograms of the age of
the male and of the female population (5-year classes from 0 to 105 years).
With only two variables a flower has two opposite petals: the male population
on the right, the female one on the left, the age growing from the centre
outwards. It is a population pyramid lying on its side.

```{r}
countries <- c("Niger", "Nigeria", "India", "Brazil", "China", "United States",
               "Italy", "Japan")
Ages <- Age_Pyramids_2014[match(countries, rownames(Age_Pyramids_2014@M)), 2:3]
colnames(Ages@M) <- c("Male", "Female")
```

The range of the colours and of the stems is set to the whole age range with
`ranges = c(0, 105)`, and 21 classes match the 5-year classes of the data.

### How wide is a petal? `width_type`

In the original design of the flower plot the width of a petal is an
*angle*: a petal far from the centre is wider than a petal of the same
probability near the centre, and its area grows with the distance from the
centre. This is fine to compare the same value across units, but it distorts
the comparison along a stem: here it would inflate the old ages. With
`width_type = "linear"` the width is a distance from the stem, the same at
every radius, so that it is exactly proportional to the probability. Compare
the two versions for Niger and Japan:

```{r, fig.height = 2.8}
flower_grid(Ages, rows = c("Niger", "Japan"), ncol = 2, n_levels = 21,
            ranges = c(0, 105), palette = "Viridis", labels = TRUE,
            width_type = "angular")
flower_grid(Ages, rows = c("Niger", "Japan"), ncol = 2, n_levels = 21,
            ranges = c(0, 105), palette = "Viridis", labels = TRUE,
            width_type = "linear")
```

With angular widths the Japanese petals look heavier at the old ages than
they are, and the Nigerien petals look thinner at the young ages than they
are. With linear widths the petals are proper pyramids: half of the
population of Niger is younger than 15 years, against 13% in Japan, where a
quarter of the population is 65 or older.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
flower_grid(Ages, ncol = 4, n_levels = 21, ranges = c(0, 105),
            palette = "Viridis", labels = TRUE, width_type = "linear")
```

From Niger to Japan the flowers show the demographic transition: the petals
move from a wide base near the centre (many children, few old people) to a
wide body at the middle ages and beyond, with the purple of the young ages
shrinking and the green and yellow of the adult and old ages growing.

## The summer climate of Chinese stations

`China_Seas` contains, for 60 meteorological stations, the histograms of
several climatic variables in each season. We take six summer variables,
measured on different scales: mean temperature (°C), total precipitation
(mm), relative humidity (%), sunshine duration (hours), wind speed (m/s) and
cloud amount (%).

```{r}
vs <- c("mean.temp_Summer", "tot.precip_Summer", "mean.rel.hum_Summer",
        "sunshine.dur_Summer", "mean.wind.speed_Summer", "mean.cloud.amount_Summer")
Summer <- China_Seas[, match(vs, colnames(China_Seas@M))]
colnames(Summer@M) <- c("temperature", "precipitation", "humidity", "sunshine",
                        "wind", "clouds")
rownames(Summer@M) <- sub("_[0-9]+$", "", rownames(Summer@M))
```

Each variable keeps its own range (the default `scheme = "variable"`): the
distance from the centre is the position of a value among all the stations,
from the lowest (near the centre, blue) to the highest (at the end of the
stem, red). The petals are ordered by the shortest Hamiltonian cycle through
the variables (`var_order = "tsp"`).

### Which petal is the widest? `width_scale`

The width of the petals is relative to the widest one. By default
(`width_scale = "common"`) the widest petal of the whole plot sets the scale.
With very different variables this is a problem: the temperature of a
southern station in summer changes by less than one degree from year to year,
so its petal is very concentrated, very wide, and makes all the other petals
thin. With `width_scale = "variable"` each variable has its own scale: widths
are comparable across stations for the same variable, and every variable uses
all the space of its sector.

```{r, fig.height = 5.6}
stations <- c("Hailaer", "WuLuMuQi", "HaMi", "LaSa", "BeiJing", "ShangHai",
              "KunMing", "HaiKou")
flower_grid(Summer, rows = stations, ncol = 4, palette = "Zissou 1", labels = TRUE,
            var_order = "tsp", width_type = "linear", width_scale = "variable")
```

Each station has a recognisable shape:

* **HaMi** and **WuLuMuQi**, in the deserts of the north-west, have the
  precipitation, humidity and cloud petals close to the centre and the
  sunshine petal at the end of its stem (HaMi has the driest and sunniest
  summer of the 60 stations);
* **HaiKou**, on the tropical island of Hainan, is the opposite: temperature,
  precipitation and humidity far from the centre; its temperature petal is a
  thin, wide sliver because the summer temperature hardly changes from year
  to year;
* **KunMing** and **LaSa**, on the high plateaus of the south-west, have
  cool summers (temperature petals near the centre) and many clouds; KunMing
  has one of the least sunny summers;
* **ShangHai** stands out for the wind, the strongest of the selected
  stations.

The means and the ranks (1 = lowest of the 60 stations) confirm the
reading:

```{r}
m <- get.MatH.stats(Summer, stat = "mean")$mat
cbind(round(m[stations, c("temperature", "precipitation", "sunshine")], 1),
      rank_sunshine = rank(m[, "sunshine"])[match(stations, rownames(m))])
```

### All the stations, grouped by cluster

As the other plots of the package, flowers can be grouped by a clustering.
Here the 60 stations are grouped by a Ward clustering of the six summer
histograms (computed on the original histograms by `dv_cluster()`), without
names around the flowers:

```{r, fig.height = 9}
dv <- dv_data(Summer, n_levels = 30)
cl <- dv_cluster(dv, cols = FALSE)
flower_grid(dv, groups = cutree(cl$hc_rows, 4), ncol = 8, palette = "Zissou 1",
            var_order = "tsp", width_type = "linear", width_scale = "variable",
            center = "plain")
```

Cluster 2 collects the six stations of the arid north-west (Yi Ning,
WuLuMuQi, HaMi, Jiu Quan, ZhangYe, YinChuan), whose flowers have the rain,
humidity and cloud petals close to the centre; cluster 4 five stations of the
south-eastern coast (WenZhou, GuangZhou, ShanTou, ZhanJiang, HaiKou), hot and
wet; clusters 1 and 3 split the rest of the country.

### On the map

`flower_pca()` places each flower at given coordinates; with the longitude and
the latitude of the stations and a map of China in the background
(`basemap`, here from `ggplot2::map_data()`, which needs the **maps** package)
the flowers are centred on their stations. `key_position` puts the key flower,
the barycenter of the 60 stations, in an empty corner of the map.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE), fig.height = 6.2}
lonlat <- with(stations_coordinates,
               cbind(longitude = LON.deg + LON.min / 60, latitude = LAT.deg + LAT.min / 60))
rownames(lonlat) <- rownames(Summer@M)
china <- ggplot2::map_data("world", region = c("China", "Taiwan"))
flower_pca(Summer, lonlat, basemap = china, axis_titles = c("longitude", "latitude"),
           size = 0.1, palette = "Zissou 1", var_order = "tsp", width_type = "linear",
           width_scale = "variable", center = "plain", label_size = 1.8,
           key_position = c(78, 22), key_size = 0.14)
```

On the map the regional patterns emerge without any clustering: the flowers
of the north-west have the sunshine petal at the end of the stem and the rain
and cloud petals close to the centre; going south-east the rain, humidity and
temperature petals move outwards.

## Summary of the options for histogram data

| option | what it does | suggestion for histograms |
|---|---|---|
| `n_levels` | classes used to discretize the histograms | 30 (default) to 60 |
| `smooth` | smoothing of the profile of the violins (in classes) | 1.5 (default); 0 to see the raw classes |
| `width_type` | angular (original design) or linear widths | `"linear"` when values along a stem are compared |
| `width_scale` | which petal sets the width: overall, per unit, per variable | `"variable"` for variables with very different distributions |
| `ranges`, `scheme` | range of the stems and of the colours | a common range for variables on the same scale (ages, temperatures) |
| `var_order` | order of the petals | `"tsp"` to put correlated variables side by side |
| `style`, `center`, `palette` | look of the flower | `style = "light"` for print |
| `flower_pca(pca, basemap, key_position)` | flowers on a factorial plane or on a map | coordinates of the units as a two-column matrix |
